project.name: Flash-sale shop (demo, fixed version)
project.summary: A one-page flash sale for 100 pairs of limited-edition sneakers at $49.99, one pair per customer. Shoppers sign in, enter a shipping address and press Buy; the sale opens at midnight after an email blast. This is the `fixed/` version of this repository's demo, after two rounds of review and fixes.
project.author: The demo team (this repository)
project.riskReason: the app calls the card provider's charge API itself, so amounts, repeat-safety, time-outs and reconciliation are its own job, and the whole sale happens in a promoted 60-second rush.
project.reviewer: Claude Code (launch-review skill), in sessions that had not written the code and never saw the answer key

verdict.reason: One High problem is open at risk tier 3: the opening time can silently be wrong (ARC-11). The real card payment and sign-in aren't in the code, so the money flow has never been tested end to end, and no demo can clear that. Everything the previous review asked for is fixed and verified.

blockers.text: Make the opening time impossible to set wrong: one source of truth, only full times with a time zone, and show the time in force.
Hand over the production sign-in and card-payment integrations for review, then make one real small purchase and refund.
Show a tested restore, an alert that reached a named on-call person, and the on-call rota (mandatory at tier 3).
Build the operator tools the runbook relies on, and fix or replace its rollback step.

conditions.text: Run one app instance only, with the load balancer's idle timeout below 65 seconds.
Start production through a real start command that sets `NODE_ENV=production`.
Repeat the load test on production-sized machines, with the load generator on a separate machine.
Add an agent instruction file and tests for the recurring problems in §12 before the next round of AI-written fixes.

product.users: Public shoppers (about 3,000 in the first 60 seconds), the small team running the sale, and admins with a shared token.

journeys.name: Buy one pair
journeys.who: A signed-in shopper, sale open, pairs in stock
steps: Sign in with an email address (a test sign-in in the demo; a magic link in production).
journeys.expected: "Order #… confirmed — $49.99 charged." One order, one charge, at the listed price.

evidence.caption: After pressing Buy now. The sign-in box above "Signed in as…" should have disappeared (ARC-15).

journeys.name: Arrive before the sale opens
steps: Open the sale page before the opening time.
Sign in and enter an address.
journeys.expected: The page says when the sale opens and the button reads "Not open yet". A purchase sent directly to the server is refused.

evidence.caption: Before opening: the time is shown and Buy is disabled.

journeys.name: Double-click Buy
journeys.who: A signed-in shopper who clicks twice
steps: Sign in and enter an address.
journeys.expected: Exactly one order and one charge. The second click is told the shopper already has an order.

evidence.caption: After a double click: one order.

journeys.name: Pay while the payment provider is slow
journeys.who: A signed-in shopper while the provider isn't answering
steps: Press **Buy now** while the payment provider is slow or down.
journeys.expected: Within 5 seconds: "confirming your payment, please don't pay again". When the provider recovers: exactly one paid order and one charge.

evidence.caption: Provider down: the order shows as confirming, not failed.

journeys.name: Sold out
journeys.who: Any visitor after the last pair is sold
steps: Open the sale page when stock is 0.
journeys.expected: "Sold out" is shown and the button can't be pressed.

architecture.summary: One Node.js process with no framework and no third-party packages, behind a load balancer. It keeps orders in hosted Postgres (simulated), calls the payment provider directly with one repeat-safe key per order, and runs two background jobs: one settles payments whose outcome is unknown, the other sends confirmation emails from a queue in the database.
architecture.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Shopper["Shopper's browser"] -->|HTTPS| LB["Load balancer"]
  Admin["Staff: shared admin token"] -->|HTTPS| LB
  LB --> App["Node.js app (one instance)"]
  App -->|"pool of 10, 1 s wait"| DB[("Postgres: orders, stock, settings, email queue")]
  App -->|"3 s limit, key per order"| Pay["Payment provider"]
  Recon["Reconciler, every 5 s"] --> DB
  Recon -->|"same key"| Pay
  Mailer["Email sender, every 1 s"] --> DB
  Mailer -.->|"not built yet"| Mail["Email provider"]
  IdP["Sign-in provider (not in repo)"] -.-> Shopper

history.period: Three reviews, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-17, and the git history of `demo/flash-sale/` (10 commits, 2026-10-16 to 2026-10-18).
sources: Three review reports on this app: the first version (30 findings), round 1 (23) and round 2 (all 23 re-checked, plus 13 new): `demo/flash-sale/sample-reports/`.

Git history of `demo/flash-sale/`, scanned with `history-scan.mjs`: 10 commits, all with an AI co-author. Five look like fixes, but the two that matter bundle a whole round each (79 and 29 files), so git can't separate individual defects here and the review reports are the defect record.
No issue tracker or incident log exists for the demo.

stats.label: Kinds of problem that came back
Files in the biggest fix commit

classes.name: Outside calls whose outcome is unknown

occurrences.text: No time limit on the payment call: one slow charge holds the request for 30 s.
A time-out was treated as a failure: 57 charges for 39 pairs.
Database busy right after payment: the shopper is told "very busy" and the paid order is stuck.
An error that retrying can't fix leaves orders "confirming" forever.

classes.rootCause: Every outside call was modelled as success or failure. "Unknown" (timed out, but the provider may still have charged) wasn't a state, so each fix moved the problem: no time limit, then a time-out treated as failure, then "unknown" with no deadline. The tests' payment stub never completed a charge after the app gave up, so the tests couldn't see it.
classes.control: A realistic payment simulator (finishes abandoned charges, hangs 2% of calls), used by acceptance test AC-08 in CI and by the slow-provider runs.
classes.controlCheck: AC-08 fails on the round-1 code and passes on round 2; slow provider: 40 charges for 40 orders.
classes.agentRule: Every outside call: a time limit, a repeat-safe key, and an explicit "unknown" state settled by the reconciler with the same key, with a deadline.

classes.name: Bad input crashes the app or is quietly accepted

occurrences.text: Malformed JSON crashes the whole site.
A malformed Host header crashes the server.
One `GET //` crashes the shop. Introduced by the fix for the Host header.
A request body of `null` gives a 500 error.
"Nov 27" is accepted as 27 November 2001 and opens the sale.
The address check drops every non-Latin letter, so different addresses collide.

classes.rootCause: Each handler parses its own input with forgiving built-ins (`new URL`, `JSON.parse`, `new Date`, a regular expression), and each fix patched the one input that failed. There is no single validation layer and no test that sends malformed input.
classes.control: Code-scanning rules `url-parse-outside-try` and `json-parse-in-stream-callback`; the reviewer's malformed-path script (7 paths, all answered 400).
classes.controlCheck: The rules' own tests run in CI, but the rules aren't run against the app in CI, and the malformed-input script isn't in the test suite.
classes.agentRule: Parse every input once, strictly, at the edge; refuse rather than guess; add each new input to the malformed-input test.

classes.name: Settings and data that must survive restarts and deploys

occurrences.text: Every start-up recreates the database and deletes all orders.
Settings and secrets live in the code.
Every start still deletes all orders and resets stock.
A one-call "delete every order" endpoint ships to production.
Test sign-in and demo secrets can reach production.
Changing `SALE_STARTS_AT` after the first start does nothing, while the log says it did. Introduced by the round-2 fix.
Rolling back to the previous release fails against the new database. Introduced by the round-2 migrations.

classes.rootCause: Start-up, settings and deploy behaviour was never specified or tested. Every test starts a fresh app on an empty in-memory database, so the second start, start-up with old data, and the previous release were invisible.
classes.control: Versioned migrations; production refuses demo switches and placeholder secrets; the reviewer's restart script with a saved database.
classes.controlCheck: A restart keeps orders (verified in round 2), but no restart or rollback test runs in CI, and ARC-11 and OPS-09 are still open.
classes.agentRule: Any change to start-up, settings or the database needs a test that starts the app twice on the same data, and one that starts the previous release.

classes.name: Business rules checked in code instead of enforced by the database

occurrences.text: Stock is read, then written back: 1,962 pairs sold out of 100.
No one-per-customer limit and no repeat-safety: 963 shoppers charged twice.
No database constraints for any business rule.
The price is taken from the browser.
"One per customer" is really one per email address.
Still easy to get round, and nothing slows bots down.

classes.rootCause: Rules were written as checks inside request handlers, which simultaneous requests and small variations slip past. Once moved into atomic updates and unique indexes they held; the identity behind "one per customer" is still weak.
classes.control: Atomic stock update, unique indexes and `CHECK (stock >= 0)`, with the race test in CI.
classes.controlCheck: Race test in CI on every change: 1,000 buyers, 100 sold, 0 charged twice.
classes.agentRule: Enforce limits with constraints or atomic updates, never check-then-write; the race test must pass.

classes.name: Screen behaviour no test looked at closely

occurrences.text: The page gets stuck when the server is busy or the session has expired.
Pairs returned after a failed payment are never offered again (found by a test).
The sign-in box never disappears; it has been there since the first version.
A countdown longer than about 25 days reloads the page non-stop. Introduced with the round-2 countdown.
The page points to an order history and an email that don't exist.

classes.rootCause: The acceptance tests check what should appear, never what should disappear or change, and nothing tests the page's timers and error paths. The page was reviewed through the server's eyes.
classes.control: Guidance "assert what should disappear, too" added to the acceptance-test skill.
classes.controlCheck: Not applied to this suite yet: no test checks that the sign-in box hides.
classes.agentRule: For every change of state on the page, test what appears and what disappears.

classes.name: Operations promised on paper but not in tools

occurrences.text: No error tracking, uptime monitoring or alerts.
No backups or recovery.
The launch-night safety nets aren't in evidence.
Still listed in the runbook, still not shown.
The runbook relies on tools that don't exist: loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses, comparing charges with orders.

classes.rootCause: Operations were written down as intentions (a runbook, a checklist) but never rehearsed, so missing tools and broken steps stayed invisible until a reviewer tried them.
classes.control: Checklist rule: every runbook step must be backed by a tool that exists and has been tried.
classes.controlCheck: No rehearsal has been run yet.
classes.agentRule: Don't add a runbook step without the command that performs it and a log of it being tried.

areaNotes.R: A reviewer can run the app and its tests from the README in minutes. What's missing is a staging copy and any agreed figure for acceptable data loss and recovery time.
areaNotes.H: The tests that exist are good: they check outcomes, cover payment failures and double clicks, and pass reliably in CI. What's missing is the layer that keeps the next AI-written change on track: there are no instructions for coding agents, no test sends malformed input or restarts the app (two problems that came back), and nothing lints or type-checks the server.
areaNotes.A: A deliberately small design: one process, no packages, every decision on the server. It handles slow payments correctly now. The weak points are the opening time, which can be silently wrong, and a rollback that fails.
areaNotes.D: Stock, duplicates and the price are enforced by the database and proven by a 1,000-buyer race. The gaps are input that's accepted when it should be refused (the opening time) and payments that can stay "confirming" forever.
areaNotes.S: Access to orders, injection, secrets and error messages are sound, and test-only routes are refused in production. Still open: a shared admin password, a weak one-per-customer identity with no bot protection, and the production sign-in, which isn't in the code to review.
areaNotes.P: The expected rush passes in every run with a lot of room to spare, the race never oversold, and a slow payment provider no longer causes double charges. Capacity above 150% isn't proven, because everything ran on one laptop-class machine.
areaNotes.O: Health checks, safe restarts and the pause switch work. Backups, alerts, the on-call rota and the runbook's tools haven't been shown, and the documented rollback fails.
areaNotes.Q: Six kinds of problem came back across three reviews, and five problems were introduced by fixes. Two kinds are now caught automatically in CI; the other four still depend on a reviewer noticing.
areaNotes.U: Every agreed criterion passes three runs in a row, with screenshots. The criteria were agreed before testing and re-approved when they changed.

findings.title: The opening time can silently be wrong
findings.impact: If the opening time is changed after the first start, the server keeps the old one while its log shows the new one, so the sale can open hours early or stay shut at midnight. A date without a time zone, or text like "Nov 27" (read as 2001), opens the sale at once.
findings.fix: One source of truth, only full times with a time zone, and show the time in force in the log and the admin answer. Effort: small.

findings.title: A payment that never resolves stays "confirming" forever
findings.impact: A payment error that retrying can't fix keeps the pair reserved indefinitely; the whole stock could be locked with nothing sold, and the first alert comes after 10 minutes.
findings.fix: Look the payment up instead of re-sending it, give "confirming" a deadline, then release the pair and tell the shopper.

findings.title: One person can still buy several pairs, and nothing slows bots
findings.impact: A second mailbox or a re-spelt address buys another pair.
findings.fix: Firmer identity for the limit, and a waiting room or bot protection in front of the drop.

findings.title: Production safety depends on one setting nobody sets
findings.impact: Started without `NODE_ENV=production`, the shop runs with demo secrets, test sign-in and the reset route switched on.
findings.fix: A real production start command that sets it, and a start-up check that refuses demo values.

findings.title: One shared admin password, and no record of who used it
findings.impact: Anyone with the token can open, move or pause the sale, and the log can't say who did.
findings.fix: Personal admin accounts and an audit entry per change.

findings.title: Rate limits live in one server
findings.impact: A second instance would halve the protection.
findings.fix: Run one instance (runbook), or move limits to a shared store first.

findings.title: Confirmation emails are queued but never sent
findings.impact: Shoppers get no confirmation.
findings.fix: Connect the email provider, with retries per email.

findings.title: One signed-in script can tie up the database
findings.impact: Unlimited signed-in reads can starve checkout during the rush.
findings.fix: Rate-limit signed-in reads.

findings.title: The page reloads non-stop if the sale is more than ~25 days away
findings.impact: Browser timers overflow, so every open page hammers the server.
findings.fix: Cap the countdown timer and re-check periodically.

findings.title: Signing in early doesn't survive a new tab
findings.impact: Shoppers who sign in before midnight and open a new tab must sign in again during the rush.
findings.fix: Keep the session across tabs.

findings.title: The launch-night safety nets haven't been shown
findings.impact: Backups, error tracking, alerts and on-call are listed in the runbook but not evidenced.
findings.fix: Show a tested restore, a received test alert and the rota.

findings.title: The runbook relies on tools that don't exist
findings.impact: Loading stock, resolving a stuck payment, exporting addresses and comparing charges with orders have no tool.
findings.fix: Build each tool and try it once.

findings.title: Rolling back to the previous release fails
findings.impact: The rollback the runbook prescribes fails at start-up, so the shop stays down when things are already bad.
findings.fix: Make the previous release start against the new schema, or roll forward with a tested fix.

findings.title: No request ids, and admin actions are anonymous
findings.impact: Harder to trace one shopper's problem.
findings.fix: A request id per request, and admin identity in the log.

findings.title: Different non-Latin addresses collide
findings.impact: A shopper with an address in Japanese, Russian or Greek can be refused because of someone else's address.
findings.fix: Normalise with Unicode-aware rules.

findings.title: One failing email would block the rest
findings.impact: Once real sending is added.
findings.fix: Retry per email.

findings.title: The page points to things that don't exist
findings.impact: Shoppers are sent to an order history and an email that don't exist.
findings.fix: Remove or build them.

findings.title: The sign-in box never hides, and the stock count is stale after buying
findings.impact: Confusing during a one-minute sale; some shoppers will sign in again.
findings.fix: Fix the CSS rule that overrides `hidden`, and add a test that it disappears.

findings.title: The product cache drops its last good copy when the database is slow
findings.impact: Slow database means slow pages for everyone.
findings.fix: Serve the last good copy while refreshing.

findings.title: Any `?v=` value is cached for a year
findings.impact: A mixed-version deploy can pin old JavaScript.
findings.fix: Cache only the current hash.

findings.title: No instructions for the AI agents that write the code
findings.impact: Every new agent session starts without the project's rules and lessons, so the problems in §12 can return. Five problems so far were introduced by fixes.
findings.fix: Add a short AGENTS.md: how to start and test, the seven business rules, where money and secrets are handled, never edit applied migrations, and one rule per recurring problem linked to its test. Effort: small.

findings.title: Two recurring problems have no test: bad input and restarts
findings.impact: Crashes from bad input came back twice, and start-up and settings problems came back four times; each time only a reviewer caught them.
findings.fix: Move the review's malformed-input and restart scripts into the CI suite, and add a lint and type check for the server. Effort: medium.

findings.title: Four of six recurring problems have no automatic control
findings.impact: They depend on the next reviewer noticing.
findings.fix: One control per problem class, each proven against a past example.
